topic: Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement is the law of conservation of mass?
items.correct: No atoms are lost or made, so the products have the same mass as the reactants.
items.misconception: Atoms are destroyed when a gas escapes, so the mass of the products falls.
items.why: Students trust the balance over the law. A gas is invisible and disperses, so it stops feeling like a substance at all, and the falling reading looks like direct evidence that matter has disappeared. Ask where the atoms went, not where the mass went. Every carbon and oxygen atom in the escaping gas came from the marble and the acid and still exists; the balance simply no longer has them on it.
items.random_wrong: The masses are equal only when the reaction happens in a sealed container.

items.q: 4.8 g of magnesium is heated in air and reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen. What is the mass of magnesium oxide formed?
items.why: Gases cannot be seen or felt, and they rise out of the apparatus, which looks like the behaviour of something with no weight. Nothing in everyday experience makes the mass of air obvious. Point to the numbers. The mass that disappeared from the balance is exactly the mass of gas made, which is only possible if the gas particles carry that mass with them.

items.q: Which equation for the reaction of sodium with water is correctly balanced?
items.correct: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
items.misconception: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
items.why: Students match what they can see quickly. Comparing whole formulae is far easier than counting atoms element by element, and it gives the right answer often enough to feel reliable. Insist on an atom tally for each element, written out under the equation. Balancing is defined in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element on both sides, not the numbers of formulae.

items.q: A student tries to balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by rewriting the product as H₂O₂. Why is this not acceptable?
items.correct: H₂O₂ is a different substance, so the equation no longer shows this reaction.
items.misconception: It is allowed as long as the same subscript change is made on the other side.
items.why: Balancing is met as an arithmetic puzzle, and the subscripts are the numbers most easily adjusted to make the sums work. The chemical meaning of a formula gets lost behind the counting. Ask what H₂O₂ is. It is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance with different properties. Changing a subscript changes the chemical, so the equation is no longer about the reaction being described.
items.random_wrong: The atoms now balance, but the equation shows too many molecules.

items.q: How many atoms in total are shown by 2Ca(OH)₂?
items.why: The multiplier sits directly against the first symbol, so it reads as belonging to that symbol alone, the way an adjective attaches to the nearest noun. Read the multiplier as 'two lots of the whole formula'. Write the formula out twice if necessary: MgCl₂ MgCl₂ makes 2 Mg and 4 Cl unmistakable.

items.q: In the equation 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what does the 2 written in front of MgO tell you?
items.correct: Two units of magnesium oxide: two Mg atoms and two O atoms.
items.misconception: Two extra oxygen atoms are joined to each magnesium oxide.
items.why: Balancing is met as an arithmetic puzzle, and the subscripts are the numbers most easily adjusted to make the sums work. The chemical meaning of a formula gets lost behind the counting. Ask what H₂O₂ is. It is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance with different properties. Changing a subscript changes the chemical, so the equation is no longer about the reaction being described.
items.random_wrong: Twice as much magnesium oxide forms, by mass, as magnesium.

items.q: What is the relative formula mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)
items.why: Students read the formula as a list of ingredients rather than as a count of atoms, and the subscript is small and easily skipped when the periodic table values are being copied out. Write the atom count beside each symbol before adding anything. Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula, so each subscript must multiply its own Ar.

items.q: What is the relative formula mass of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂? (Ar: Mg 24, N 14, O 16)
items.why: Every other subscript students meet does apply to the single symbol on its left, so the rule is generalised straight past the bracket without noticing that the bracket has changed what it is attached to. Treat the bracket as one parcel. Whatever is inside it is repeated as many times as the subscript says, so Mg(NO₃)₂ is Mg with two complete NO₃ groups.

items.q: 50 g of calcium carbonate is heated in an open tube until it fully decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The calcium oxide left has a mass of 28 g. What mass of carbon dioxide escaped?
items.why: The totals on each side really do behave like masses, and questions often go on to use grams, so students collapse the distinction between a relative mass and a measured mass. Keep the two apart. The equation fixes the ratio in which relative masses combine; grams only appear once an actual quantity is stated in the question.

items.q: In a balanced equation, why does the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants equal that of the products?
items.correct: The same atoms are present on both sides, just rearranged, so the totals match.
items.misconception: Every reaction is done in a sealed container, so nothing at all can escape.
items.why: Every demonstration that shows constant mass uses a stoppered flask, so the seal is remembered as a condition for the law rather than as a way of keeping the products where they can be weighed. Name the system. Mass is conserved for the reaction as a whole; the seal only decides whether all the products stay on the balance. Weigh the escaping gas too and the total is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: The balancing numbers are chosen to make the two mass totals come out equal.

items.q: Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, has a relative formula mass of 100. What is the percentage by mass of oxygen in it? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)
items.why: Percentage is met first as a share of a count, and counting atoms in a formula is quicker than working with relative atomic masses. The method feels right because it does produce a sensible-looking percentage. Ask which is heavier, an oxygen atom or a calcium atom. Since atoms differ in mass, a share of the atoms is not a share of the mass; only masses may be divided by masses.

items.q: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, has a relative formula mass of 80. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in it? (Ar: N 14, H 1, O 16)
items.why: The relative atomic mass is copied straight from the periodic table, and the subscript is treated as part of the formula's name rather than as a count that belongs in the calculation. Build the numerator in two steps, always: the Ar of the element multiplied by how many of its atoms the formula shows. The denominator is the Mr, which already contains both of them.

items.q: Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, has a relative formula mass of 98. Which expression gives the percentage by mass of hydrogen in it? (Ar: H 1)
items.why: The relative atomic mass is copied straight from the periodic table, and the subscript is treated as part of the formula's name rather than as a count that belongs in the calculation. Build the numerator in two steps, always: the Ar of the element multiplied by how many of its atoms the formula shows. The denominator is the Mr, which already contains both of them.

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is heated in an open crucible until it has fully reacted. What happens to the mass of the solid, and why?
items.correct: It rises, because oxygen from the air has combined with the magnesium.
items.misconception: It falls, because the magnesium burns away and is lost into the air.
items.why: Everyday burning - wood, paper, a candle - leaves a small pile of ash, so students generalise that combustion always removes material rather than adding a reactant from the air. Compare the two cases. Wood loses mass because its gaseous products drift off; magnesium keeps its product as a solid and gains the oxygen as well, so the crucible ends heavier.
items.random_wrong: It rises, because heating expands the metal and larger pieces weigh more.

items.q: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. The mass of solid in the tube falls. Why?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide gas is produced and escapes, taking its mass away.
items.misconception: Heat from the flame has destroyed some of the carbon and oxygen atoms.
items.why: Students trust the balance over the law. A gas is invisible and disperses, so it stops feeling like a substance at all, and the falling reading looks like direct evidence that matter has disappeared. Ask where the atoms went, not where the mass went. Every carbon and oxygen atom in the escaping gas came from the marble and the acid and still exists; the balance simply no longer has them on it.
items.random_wrong: The solid evaporates, so copper carbonate is lost from the tube as vapour.

items.q: In an open flask on a balance, calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The reading falls. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Mass is conserved; the carbon dioxide has left and is no longer weighed.
items.misconception: Mass is not conserved here, because the flask was not sealed with a bung.
items.why: Every demonstration that shows constant mass uses a stoppered flask, so the seal is remembered as a condition for the law rather than as a way of keeping the products where they can be weighed. Name the system. Mass is conserved for the reaction as a whole; the seal only decides whether all the products stay on the balance. Weigh the escaping gas too and the total is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: The carbon dioxide produced has no mass of its own, so the products weigh less.

items.q: The same reaction is repeated in a flask sealed with a bung, standing on a balance. What happens to the reading?
items.correct: It stays the same, because the carbon dioxide is still inside the flask.
items.misconception: It falls, because once the carbon is a gas its particles have no mass.
items.why: Gases cannot be seen or felt, and they rise out of the apparatus, which looks like the behaviour of something with no weight. Nothing in everyday experience makes the mass of air obvious. Point to the numbers. The mass that disappeared from the balance is exactly the mass of gas made, which is only possible if the gas particles carry that mass with them.
items.random_wrong: It rises, because the gas particles press outwards on the sealed flask.

items.q: 0.24 g of magnesium ribbon is burned in an open crucible and 0.40 g of white solid is left. Which statement explains the increase in terms of the particle model?
items.correct: Oxygen molecules from the air have bonded to magnesium in the solid.
items.misconception: The magnesium particles have grown larger as they took in heat energy.
items.why: Size and mass are bound together in everyday thinking, and expansion is the effect of heating that students recall most readily, so it is offered whenever heat and a mass change appear together. Separate the two ideas with a test: heat a solid that does not react and the balance does not move. Only a chemical change that adds or removes particles alters the mass.
items.random_wrong: Extra particles were created in the crucible as the bright flame burned.

items.q: A student measures the same volume of solution five times and gets five slightly different readings. What does this show?
items.correct: Whenever a measurement is made there is some uncertainty in the result.
items.misconception: The student was careless; accurate work gives the same value each time.
items.why: School practicals are marked for care and neatness, so disagreement between repeats is read as a personal failing rather than as a property of measurement itself. Show that even the best equipment has a smallest division and a reading judgement. Uncertainty can be reduced and estimated, but it is never removed, which is why results are quoted with a range.
items.random_wrong: A mistake has been made, so all five of the readings must be wrong.

items.q: A student records five titres: 24.10, 24.15, 24.20, 25.90 and 24.15 cm³. What should be done before estimating the uncertainty?
items.correct: Set the results out to show their distribution and treat 25.90 as anomalous.
items.misconception: Include all five of the titres in the mean, since every reading must be used.
items.why: Students are told not to fiddle with results, and excluding a value looks like exactly that. The difference between discarding an identified anomaly and discarding an inconvenient value is not obvious. Make the decision visible and justified. Display the distribution, state which value sits apart from it and why it is treated as anomalous, then calculate the mean from the rest.
items.random_wrong: Use 25.90 as the measure of spread, as it is the largest value found.

items.q: Four titres are recorded: 24.10, 24.15, 24.20 and 24.15 cm³. What is the range of these measurements?
items.correct: 0.10 cm³
items.why: In everyday speech a range is the span a thing covers, and the largest number is the most striking one on the page. Students report a value from the data instead of a difference between two of them. Make it a subtraction every time. The range measures how spread out the results are, so it must be small when they agree closely - 24.20 cm³ would say the readings differ by a whole 24 cm³.

items.q: The mean of a set of titres is 24.15 cm³ and their range is 0.10 cm³. How should the result be quoted?
items.why: The range is the number just calculated, so it is the number that gets written down. That the plus-or-minus sign covers an interval of twice that width is easy to overlook. Draw the interval on a number line. The results run from the smallest to the largest, and the mean sits between them, so the distance from the mean to each end is half the range.

items.q: Burning magnesium leaves a solid heavier than the metal. Have extra atoms been made?
items.correct: No atoms are made. Oxygen atoms from the air have joined the magnesium, so the oxide contains the mass of both the metal and the oxygen that reacted.
items.misconception: The reaction creates new material, which is why the product weighs more than what you started with.
items.why: Conservation of mass is often taught with the mass loss case only. When a reading rises instead, students reach for the opposite explanation and assume matter has been generated, since nothing visible was added. Point at the air. The reactant that raised the mass was already there as an invisible gas; weigh the crucible with a lid on and the gain still comes from oxygen entering, never from new atoms.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student balances the sodium in 2Na + H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ and stops. Is the equation finished?
items.correct: No. Oxygen and hydrogen are still unequal. Every element has to balance at the same time, which needs 2H₂O on the left.
items.misconception: Once the metal, or whichever element you dealt with first, has the same number on each side, the equation is balanced.
items.why: The first element balanced is usually the easiest one, and the sense of having solved something makes students stop checking. Nothing on the page signals that the other elements have shifted. Re-count every element after each change. Adding a multiplier to fix one element almost always disturbs another, so balancing is finished only when a full tally shows all elements equal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many hydrogen atoms are shown by 2H₂O?
items.correct: 4. The 2 in front and the subscript 2 are multiplied together, giving 2 x 2 = 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms.
items.misconception: The number in front is just a label saying how many molecules there are, so you count either it or the subscript, not both.
items.why: Two numbers of different kinds sit in one expression and students treat them as alternatives rather than factors. Only one number is usually needed in the simpler examples met first. Separate the two jobs, then combine them. The subscript says how many atoms are in one molecule; the multiplier says how many molecules there are; the atom count is the product of the two.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The Mr of CO₂ is 44. Is that 44 grams?
items.correct: No. Relative formula mass is a ratio of masses, so it has no units. It is written simply as 44.
items.misconception: Relative formula mass is a mass, so it must be measured in grams like everything else you weigh.
items.why: The word mass is in the name, and in later work the same number does appear in gram quantities. Students see a number that behaves like a mass and supply the familiar unit. Stress the word relative. Mr compares the mass of one formula unit with the relative atomic masses used to build it; a comparison has no unit, so no gram symbol is written.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student calculates the Mr of CaCO₃ as 40 + 12 + 16 + 3 = 71. Where is the error?
items.correct: The subscript 3 must multiply the Ar of oxygen, not be added to the total: 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100.
items.misconception: Every number in the formula gets added into the total, so the subscript is another number to include in the sum.
items.why: The calculation is remembered as 'add up the numbers in the formula'. Once addition is the only operation in mind, any digit on the page is treated as another term. Say what each number counts. The subscript counts atoms and the Ar gives the mass of one of them, so they multiply; only the totals for different elements are added.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how are the relative formula masses compared on the two sides?
items.correct: Include the multipliers: (2 x 2) + 32 = 36 on the left and 2 x 18 = 36 on the right. The totals are equal.
items.misconception: You compare the Mr of one formula on the left with the Mr of one formula on the right, so 2 and 32 against 18 shows they do not match.
items.why: Relative formula mass is learned for single compounds first, so the habit is to work out one formula at a time and the equation's multipliers are treated as decoration. Read the specification wording literally: the sum of the relative formula masses in the quantities shown. Each multiplier is part of the quantity, so multiply each Mr by the number in front of it before adding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do the relative formula mass totals on the two sides of a balanced equation agree?
items.correct: Because the same atoms appear on both sides, only rearranged. The multipliers are chosen to balance atoms, and equal mass totals follow from that.
items.misconception: The numbers in front of the formulae are picked so that the two mass totals come out the same.
items.why: Students see the totals match every time and infer that matching them was the goal, reversing cause and effect in a rule that always seems to work. Balance an equation without ever mentioning mass, then add the Mr totals afterwards. They agree because the atom counts agree, which is conservation of mass showing itself, not a target that was aimed at.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper carbonate is heated: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. Why does the solid lose mass?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide is produced and escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the copper oxide as the only solid product.
items.misconception: The heat destroys part of the carbonate, or the solid evaporates away as copper carbonate vapour.
items.why: Heating is associated with evaporation and with things being burnt up. Without the equation in front of them, students explain the loss with a physical change instead of naming the gas produced. Read the products off the equation. One product is a gas and the other is a solid; the gas leaves the tube and takes its mass with it, and no atoms are destroyed at any point.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gas is produced inside a sealed flask on a balance. Does the reading rise?
items.correct: No, it stays the same. The same particles are present, all still inside the flask, so the total mass on the balance is unchanged.
items.misconception: The gas particles push outwards on the sealed flask as they move, and that pressure adds to the reading.
items.why: Students know a gas exerts pressure and know a balance measures a downward force, so the two are merged. The particles pressing on the walls feels as though it should register as extra weight. Ask what has entered or left. Nothing has, so nothing on the balance has changed. Pressure acts in all directions inside the flask and does not add mass to it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an uncertainty of ± 0.05 cm³ an admission that a mistake was made?
items.correct: No. It states the interval in which the true value is expected to lie. A mistake is an error in what was done and would be corrected, not quoted.
items.misconception: Uncertainty means you got it wrong, so quoting one is owning up to sloppy work.
items.why: In ordinary English 'uncertain' means unsure or unreliable, and the word 'error' is used loosely in class for both mistakes and measurement uncertainty, so the two collapse together. Distinguish them by what you would do next. A mistake is put right and the measurement repeated; an uncertainty is estimated from the spread of good repeats and reported with the result.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
